summary: PlayCanvas is two things under one name: an open-source runtime released under the MIT licence, and a hosted editor and publishing service at playcanvas.com. The runtime is a mature real-time renderer on WebGL 2 and WebGPU, with an entity-and-component scene model, glTF 2.0 reading and writing, animation state graphs, positioned sound, WebXR sessions, and unusually deep support for Gaussian splats including level-of-detail streaming. Physics is not in the runtime: rigid bodies, collision shapes, joints and trigger volumes ship as components that stay inert until the application separately loads ammo.js, a WebAssembly port of Bullet. The runtime carries no networking, no identity, no persistence and no avatar model at all, and PlayCanvas documents multi-user work only as tutorials that wire a scene to a third-party server such as Socket.io, Colyseus or Photon. The first trap for a standards audience is the product split: reading FBX or COLLADA, baking font atlases, compressing textures, resolving template overrides and producing a runnable package are all hosted-editor jobs done on PlayCanvas servers, and none of them exist in the open-source runtime. The second trap is that several load-bearing conventions, including right-handed axes with Y up, column-major matrices and one unit to the metre, are stated in source comments or a single documentation page rather than specified anywhere normative.
